text.hook:
Most C++ memory bugs are lifetime bugs.
Interviewers test whether you can say exactly when an object dies.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Storage vs lifetime vs scope
2. When lifetime starts and ends
3. When const& extends a temporary
4. Construction and destruction order
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Storage, lifetime, temporaries and order: what interviewers actually check.

slides.title: Three ideas people blur

cards.label: Storage duration
cards.text: How long the **memory** stays reserved: automatic, static, thread, dynamic.

cards.label: Lifetime
cards.text: When the **object** exists: from end of initialization to the start of its destructor.

cards.label: Scope
cards.text: Where a **name** can be used. A `static` local: block scope, program-long lifetime.

slides.takeaway: Every dangling bug is the same bug: a non-owning handle used after its object's lifetime ended.

slides.title: Four durations, four lifetimes
rows: local `int x;`: block entry / block exit
global, `static` local: before `main` (or first pass) / after `main`
`thread_local`: first use in the thread / thread exit
slides.takeaway: `int* p = new int(5);`: `p` is automatic, `*p` is dynamic. When `p` dies, the `int` leaks.

cards.label: Starts
cards.text: When the constructor **finishes**. If it throws, the object never existed: no destructor.

cards.label: Ends
cards.text: When the destructor **starts**. A moved-from object is still alive.

cards.label: Storage can outlive it
cards.text: After `optional::reset()` or `pop_back()` the bytes remain. Using them is UB.

slides.title: Does `const&` extend the temporary?
slides.takeaway: Only a direct binding to the temporary (or its member) extends it. Never through a function call.

slides.title: Construction and destruction order
rows: destroyed in reverse of completed construction
slides.takeaway: Declare a member after everything it uses: it is then destroyed first.

slides.lead: Since C++11 exactly one thread runs the initializer, others wait. Later reads and writes still need their own synchronization.

items.myth: "Moving from an object ends its lifetime."
items.truth: It changes its state. Only destruction (`reset`, scope exit, `delete`) ends lifetime.

items.myth: "Members are initialized in the order of the initializer list."
items.truth: Declaration order. `-Wreorder` (in `-Wall`) warns about the mismatch.

items.myth: "The memory still holds the old value, so using the object is fine."
items.truth: Lifetime ended means UB, whatever the bytes say.

items.myth: "`join()` makes a pointer to the thread's local safe."
items.truth: The local died when the thread function returned. `join()` only waits.

items.myth: "`volatile` puts a variable in RAM and makes it thread-safe."
items.truth: Neither. It only affects accesses. Use `std::atomic` for threads.

items.myth: "Static objects are destroyed in declaration order."
items.truth: In reverse order of completed construction.

slides.hero:
Storage is memory.
Lifetime is when
the object exists in it.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
std::max returns a const int&.
You bind it to a const int&. Is that well-defined?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Three lines, no pointers, no heap. Still a classic dangling reference interviewers love.

slides.title:
Is this well-defined?
What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: `m` refers to a temporary `5` that died at the `;`
bullets: The literal `5` becomes a temporary bound to its parameter. `std::max` returns a reference to it.
The temporary dies at the end of the full-expression. `m` was not bound to it directly: no extension.

slides.title: Copy the value, not the reference
slides.tip: GCC 11 is silent. GCC 13 warns with `-Wdangling-reference`.
slides.takeaway: Lifetime extension never passes through a function that returns a reference.

text.hook:
A range-for over a getter of a temporary.
GCC 11 compiles it cleanly. Is it well-defined in C++20?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: One of the few lifetime bugs the language itself changed in C++23.

slides.title: C++20. What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: C++20 and earlier. C++23 (P2718) extends the temporaries: 303
bullets: `__range` binds to the reference `get()` returns, not to the `Book` temporary.
So the `Book` dies at the end of that line, before the first iteration.
A plain GCC 11 run printed 354819955. ASan: `stack-use-after-scope`.

slides.title: Keep the owner alive
slides.takeaway: Before C++23, range-for only extends what `__range` binds to directly. A getter breaks the chain.

text.hook:
This passed code review.
The vector is alive the whole time,
so the reference is fine. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: It even prints the right number in testing. That is why it survives.

slides.title: What does it print?

bullets: At `size() == capacity()`, `push_back` allocates a new block, moves every element and **destroys** the old ones.
`first` refers to an old element whose lifetime has ended.
GCC `-O0` printed 100: the freed bytes were not overwritten yet. ASan: `heap-use-after-free`.
`const&` extends only a temporary. `orders[0]` is an existing element.

slides.title: Keep an index, not a reference
slides.tip: `reserve(n)` up front also works, but only when the bound is really known.
slides.takeaway: A reference into a `std::vector` survives only until the next reallocation. Same bug: `push_back` inside a range-for over the same vector.

text.hook:
Two globals in two .cpp files. One reads the other.
It printed 9001 in every test.
Is that guaranteed?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: No threads, no pointers, no warnings. Then someone changes the build.

slides.title: What does `main` print?

bullets: Dynamic initialization across files runs in an **unspecified** order.
Read too early, `base_port` is still zero-initialized: 0 + 1 = 1.
For class types (a global `std::string`) it is an object not yet alive: UB.
The `extern` declaration links fine. The problem is the run-time order.

slides.title: Initialize on first use
slides.tip: For constants: `constexpr` or `constinit` (C++20) need no run-time order at all.
slides.takeaway: Across files, dynamic static initialization has no order you can rely on. Mirror image: the destruction order fiasco at exit.
